channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: October flash PMIs show euro-area activity at 51.9, the lowest since June, with German manufacturing up to 54.2 and its composite down to 52.8, the UK composite at an eight-month high of 53.1 and Japan's manufacturing PMI at 53.3.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that the preliminary euro-area manufacturing PMI fell to 52.4 in October from 52.9 in September, the lowest in three months and below the expected 52.7, and that the composite fell to 51.9 from 53.1, the lowest since June, with services at 51.7 from 53.0. The Economic Times says euro-area business activity grew more slowly, restrained by a contraction in France, where protests have turned into rioting and looting, and that Germany recorded a fourth straight month above 50, helped by manufacturers doing better than expected. Il Sole 24 Ore gives Germany's composite at 52.8 from 53.8, services at 51.7 from 52.9 and manufacturing at 54.2 from 53.9, with manufacturing output down from 56 to 55.1 and new orders still rising but at the weakest pace in three months. It gives the UK composite at an eight-month high of 53.1 from 52, manufacturing at 52.8 from 51.9 and manufacturing output at 53.1, a more than two-year high, with growth the fastest since February on a rebound in new orders. For Japan, Channel News Asia says the manufacturing PMI fell to 53.3 from 54.1, the slowest expansion in seven months, with output and new-order growth easing, while services rose to 52.0 from 51.3 and the composite output index stayed at 52.3. The rows do not give the French index level, the euro-area new-orders index, or a comparison with the same month a year earlier.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give survey indices, not output figures. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, slower euro-area growth with a contraction in France and still-growing German manufacturing points to uneven demand across Europe, and slower growth in new orders in Germany could slow industrial demand later. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, manufacturing and construction customers set the demand for materials, so uneven activity could affect orders by country and sector, while the rows give no figures for them. Points that may be worth considering include the final PMI readings, new orders in Germany, and the development in France.

Commercial Times | The Economic Times | Il Sole 24 Ore | Il Sole 24 Ore | Channel News Asia

item.title: Trump determined on 22 October that petroleum production and refining are essential to national defence and invoked part of the Defense Production Act, which allows financial incentives for oil-related activities, pipelines and liquid fuel storage.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that on 22 October President Donald Trump determined, in a presidential memo, that petroleum production, refining and related activities are essential to national defence, a move that it says could open up US funding for fossil fuel projects. It says the memo also invoked part of the Cold War-era Defense Production Act, which allows the president to provide financial incentives for oil-related activities, pipelines and the storage of liquid fuels. The row says that prices for crude oil and diesel have surged since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, that the conflict has limited energy shipments globally, and that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have made fuel shortages worse. The row does not give the amount of funding, the projects or companies that could receive it, a timetable, or any effect on prices or output.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a determination and the legal basis for incentives, not an amount or a project. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, incentives for production, refining and storage aim to raise US supply or resilience over the medium term, and their effect on prices depends on how much money is made available and how fast projects are built. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, oil and gas derivatives are raw-material inputs and fuel is an energy cost, so more US supply or refining capacity could ease some input costs over time, while the row gives no figures and no effect on chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include the funding amounts and recipients, any change in US crude and diesel prices, and whether other countries adopt similar measures.

MarketScreener

item.title: Lula won Brazil's presidential runoff on 25 October with about 51.8% of the vote, Flávio Bolsonaro called for the result to be annulled, and Brazilian real futures fell nearly 10% in early Asian trade on Monday.
item.description:
People's Daily Online reports that incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the presidential election with 51.79% of the valid votes against 48.21% for Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party, according to the official tally; Chinatimes gives Lula 51.76% with 99.80% of votes counted and says he takes office on 5 January 2027. People's Daily says Lula vowed to work with the conservative Congress and to strengthen digital regulation, while Bolsonaro said it is "impossible" to recognise the results and called for the election to be annulled; Lianhe Zaobao says he argues that the Supreme Court temporarily changed the rules during the voting. MarketScreener calls the result an upset and reports that the front-month Brazilian real futures contract weakened nearly 10% against the dollar in early Asian trade on Monday, according to CME data, and that exchange-traded funds tracking Brazilian stocks in Japan and China were down 10% to 14%; it cites a Janus Henderson Investors report as saying a Bolsonaro win had been seen as the more market-friendly outcome. A second MarketScreener row says the new term faces five main economic challenges and cites public debt above 82% of GDP, up by more than 10 percentage points during Lula's current term; inflation of 4.6%, above the tolerance range of 1.5% to 4.5% even with interest rates at 13.75%; and budget targets made harder by a promise to raise the minimum wage faster than inflation. The Economic Times says the result may define Latin America's relations with the US, trade relations and the Amazon. The rows do not give the size of the market moves at a closing price, any court ruling on the annulment request, or any trade policy of the new government.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report an election result, a contested reaction and moves in futures and exchange-traded funds in Asian trading, not a change in policy or in trade flows. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a weaker real raises the cost of imported materials for Brazilian buyers and lowers the dollar value of Brazilian earnings, and a contested result can add political uncertainty to investment decisions. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Brazil is a market for construction and manufacturing materials, so currency swings and fiscal policy could affect import costs and investment plans, while the rows give no figures for the sector. Points that may be worth considering include the real at the close of trading, the Brazilian budget rules, the court's handling of the annulment request, and US–Brazil trade relations.

People's Daily Online | Chinatimes | Lianhe Zaobao | MarketScreener | MarketScreener | The Economic Times

item.title: A US proclamation signed on 23 October removes plywood, some paper products, certain machinery and packing crates from the 50% additional tariffs on Canadian goods from 30 October and adds certain valves, carpets, waste products and other items.
item.description:
Xinhua reports that President Donald Trump signed a proclamation on 23 October modifying the scope of the 50% additional tariffs on certain Canadian products, effective 30 October: the additional 50% duty will be imposed on certain valves, carpets, waste products and other items, and will no longer apply to plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment and certain packing crates and boxes. Cnyes says about 100 other goods are added to the list, including cocoa powder, shampoo, carpets, canoes and wooden coffins, and that the overall trade volume of taxed goods is maintained. Handelsblatt and Lianhe Zaobao list paints, air conditioning equipment, freezers and archery equipment among the added goods and say fresh and dried seaweed is exempted; Handelsblatt says Trump added the goods to offset the exemptions. Channel News Asia and The Independent link the exemptions to Republican Senator Susan Collins, who faces a tight race in Maine two weeks before the midterm elections on 3 November. The Independent says the White House said the president was seeking to offset the burden on US commerce while better serving the public interest. The Economic Times, citing the Wall Street Journal, says the 50% tariffs were imposed in late August on about USD 20 billion of Canadian goods, about 5% of Canada's exports to the US, that Canada retaliated, and that Trump threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles in January if no agreement is reached. The rows do not give the trade value of the exempted or added goods, the customs codes, or any Canadian response.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give a change to the scope of an existing tariff, not a new rate. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, exempting plywood, paper products and packing crates lowers costs for US users of those goods, while adding other goods raises costs for their buyers, and a scope set shortly before an election can be changed again. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, wood panels, paper and packaging are applications of adhesives and paints are a coatings product, so the changes could move trade flows and costs in both directions, while the rows give no volumes. Points that may be worth considering include the customs codes in the proclamation, any Canadian response, the effect on cross-border flows of wood panels, packaging and paints, and whether the threatened doubling of tariffs on Canadian vehicles in January goes ahead.

Xinhua | Cnyes | Handelsblatt | Lianhe Zaobao | Channel News Asia | The Independent | The Economic Times

item.title: After a meeting of EU trade ministers in Dublin, member states focused on plastics, which may become the next hot topic in EU–China trade, and Trade Commissioner Šefčovič said quotas or additional tariffs may be used.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that after the EU trade ministers' meeting in Dublin, member states are focusing on the plastics industry, which it says may become the next hot topic in EU–China trade, as the EU studies more trade restriction measures to protect industries from a surge of Chinese imports. Chinatimes says member states provided the most information on the plastics industry, that the European Commission will do legal work and then approve the relevant protective measures, and that Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said on 23 October that the EU might impose import quotas or additional tariffs on more Chinese industries before further negotiations, with significant progress in the investigation of the plastics industry; when quick protection is needed, he said, the EU will consider safeguard measures instead of lengthy negotiations. A second Commercial Times row says ministers agreed on 23 October to focus on dialogue with China while expanding trade defence measures, including restricting imports of chemicals, machinery and other products, and that the EU is considering import quotas on plastic products. Euronews reports that the Commission wants to curb Chinese imports in additional sectors in upcoming talks while exploring new trade defence measures, which risks retaliation by China, and that the 9 October deal on hybrid cars is unlikely to narrow the deficit significantly. Politico reports Šefčovič as saying that EU and Chinese officials are already discussing the next sectors for trade talks and that the implementation of the latest understanding will be reviewed in January. Šefčovič puts the EU's trade deficit with China at nearly EUR 197 billion in the first half of 2026, which, he says, may break the 2022 record at this rate; Politico gives that record as EUR 397.3 billion. The rows do not give the plastic products or customs codes concerned, a quota size or tariff rate, a date for a Commission proposal, or the chemicals and machinery products named.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a focus and a set of options, not a measure: no product list, rate or date is given. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, import quotas or tariffs on plastics from China would change the supply and price of plastic materials in Europe, and retaliation by China or a shift of trade to other origins is possible. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, plastics are materials that adhesives bond and belong to a family of related raw materials, and chemicals are named alongside, so measures on those products could change raw-material costs and the choice of suppliers, while the rows do not say which products. Points that may be worth considering include the scope of any Commission proposal, the January review of the EU–China understanding, a Chinese response, and the product lists for plastics and chemicals.

Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Chinatimes | Chinatimes | Euronews | Politico Europe

item.title: German property purchase prices were close to flat in the third quarter, with condominiums up 0.3% and houses up 0.4% on a year earlier and prices a good 10% below the 2022 peak, the IW finds.
item.description:
WirtschaftsWoche reports on a study by the German Economic Institute Cologne (IW) that condominium prices in Germany rose 0.3% in the third quarter compared with a year earlier and prices of single- and two-family houses rose 0.4%. It says purchase prices have largely moved sideways since 2023 and are a good 10% below the 2022 peak, which the experts attribute to interest rates: demand for properties for sale is falling because of higher financing costs. The row gives a rise of almost 0.7 percentage points in the yield on ten-year covered bonds since the start of 2026 and of more than 1.0 percentage point for short maturities, which it links to higher inflation expectations and doubts about the sustainability of government debt, especially in the US and France. It adds that the IW expects completions in new construction to keep falling because of lower demand, while construction costs rise, which the row links to high energy consumption. Handelsblatt, also citing the IW, reports that in the seven largest cities apartments cost almost 1% less than a year earlier and houses 2.3% less, with Stuttgart down 3.9%, Berlin down 2.0% and Cologne down 1.3%, while rents are rising sharply and prices nationwide stagnated. The rows do not give transaction volumes, the size of the rent increase or the number of completions expected.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report prices, which are not the same as transactions or building activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, flat prices after a fall, higher financing costs and falling demand for properties for sale usually weigh on new building and on the renovation decisions of owners. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, residential building and renovation are customer segments, so an expected fall in completions together with rising construction costs could keep demand for materials subdued, while sharply rising rents may support renovation and conversion work, and the rows give no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include mortgage rates and bond yields, building permits and completions data, and the development of rents.

WirtschaftsWoche | Handelsblatt

item.title: Brent crude futures rose above USD 116 a barrel in trading, a high in over five months, and WTI futures to around USD 101, with Brent up nearly 4% in the week to 23 October for a third weekly rise, on concern about escalation of the US–Iran conflict.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that concern about disruption to Middle East crude supply intensified, with Brent crude futures rising above USD 116 per barrel in trading, which it describes as a new high in over five months, and with a weekly increase of nearly 4% on 23 October, the third weekly rise in a row. It says West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures rose more than 1% to around USD 101 a barrel. It quotes Giovanni Staunovo of UBS as saying that the market remains concerned that tensions could escalate and that the worst case could trigger a new round of supply disruptions, and that unstable crude flows together with high shipping costs have left the market undersupplied. A second Commercial Times row attributes the rise to concern about an escalation of the US–Iran conflict. Business Standard reports that Brent was above USD 113 a barrel after a drone strike on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah field, where output was not affected, that spot Brent and Middle East grades have held above USD 100 for two consecutive months, and that crude is up 85% in 2026. It adds that shortages of very large crude carriers and other tankers have raised shipping rates and started to hurt refinery margins. The rows differ on the levels: one gives a peak of USD 114.72 on 23 October and also a rise above USD 116 in trading, another, undated, gives above USD 117 intraday and a close of USD 116.72, so the insight uses the first row's figures. They do not give the effect on refined products or on chemical feedstocks.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report prices, analyst concern and an undersupplied market, not a measured loss of output. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a Brent price above USD 100 a barrel together with high tanker costs raises costs along the chain from fuels to petrochemical feedstocks, and a further escalation could lift prices more. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many raw materials are made from oil and gas derivatives, so a sustained high oil price could raise input costs after a delay, while the rows give no figures for chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include the Brent level in coming sessions, tanker freight rates, any US decision on action against Iran, and raw-material price announcements by suppliers.

Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Business Standard

item.title: German construction companies received 23% more orders in August than in July, led by civil engineering, while the ZDB says its 17.3% real rise on a year earlier is mainly due to civil engineering, with a few large orders.
item.description:
Handelsblatt, citing the Federal Statistical Office, reports that construction companies in Germany received 23% more orders in August than in July, with civil engineering up 31.6% and building construction up 12.4%. It adds that, adjusted for price increases, business grew by 4.9% and that the number of employees rose by 1.5% to 548,000. The Zentralverband Deutsches Baugewerbe (ZDB) reports that sales and order intake in the main construction industry in August were significantly above the previous year's level, with sales up 4.9% in real terms, order intake up 17.3% in real terms and employment 1.5% higher. Its chief executive, Felix Pakleppa, says the strong rise in order intake is mainly due to civil engineering, up 36.4% in real terms, with few large orders in individual federal states, especially Bavaria. The ZDB adds that commercial civil engineering alone rose by 64%, or EUR 1.37 billion. The Handelsblatt row does not say whether the 23% is adjusted for price, and the 23% is month-on-month while the ZDB's order figure is year-on-year, so the two are not comparable. The rows do not give the split between public and private clients, orders for residential building on their own, or the figures for earlier months.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report order intake and sales, not building starts or materials used. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, orders for civil engineering such as roads, rail or energy networks turn into construction activity over the following months, and a rise driven by a few large orders says less about demand across the sector than a broad rise would. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, building construction is a segment where adhesive technologies are widely applied, so a rise concentrated in civil engineering could support demand by less than the headline suggests, while the rows give no materials figures. Points that may be worth considering include building-construction orders on their own, the order data for the coming months, and whether the large orders come from public infrastructure programmes.

Handelsblatt | Zentralverband Deutsches Baugewerbe

item.title: Global electric vehicle sales rose 3% year on year to 15.5 million in the first nine months, with China down 13%, Europe up 30% and North America down 24%, the Alliance for Automotive Innovation reports.
item.description:
The Alliance for Automotive Innovation reports that global electric vehicle sales rose 3% year on year to 15.5 million units through September. September sales were 2.15 million units, down 2% on a year earlier and up 17% on August. It says European sales rose 39% year on year to almost 600,000 units in September, with a year-to-date rise of 30% led by strong battery-electric growth, that the UK, France, Spain, Portugal and Finland each had their highest monthly sales, and that Germany's battery-electric sales rose 61%. China's sales fell 18% in September, after an 11% fall in August, and 13% year to date, driven mainly by a 25% fall in plug-in hybrid sales, while battery-electric sales fell 6%. Chinese passenger EV exports reached a record 558,000 units in September as manufacturers relied more on overseas markets, and Chinese-built vehicles made up 29% of European plug-in hybrid sales through September, against 14% in 2025. North American sales fell 44% in September, the steepest fall of 2026, and 24% year to date. The row does not name the underlying data provider, the unit sales behind the year-to-date percentages for China, Europe and North America, or sales by manufacturer.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives sales counts and changes by region, which measure vehicles sold, not vehicles built or demand for components. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, falling sales in China and North America and rising sales in Europe move the markets in which electric vehicles are sold, and record Chinese exports increase competition for European producers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle bodies, batteries and electronics use adhesive technologies, so a regional shift in electric-vehicle volumes could move demand between plants and suppliers, while the row gives no production or materials figures. Points that may be worth considering include the regional sales data for the coming months, Chinese export volumes and destinations, and the share of European sales that is built in Europe.

Alliance for Automotive Innovation

item.title: European natural gas prices rose 6.6% on the week to EUR 93.29 per megawatt-hour on 23 October, the highest since December 2022, while Middle East LNG shipments remained about 80% below the same period last year.
item.description:
Anadolu Agency reports that European natural gas prices increased by 6.6% over the week to EUR 93.29 per megawatt-hour as of 23 October, which it describes as the highest level since December 2022. It says continued attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz added to uncertainty over when liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments from the region will return to normal, and that LNG shipments from the Middle East remain around 80% below levels seen in the same period last year. It adds that the limited capacity of alternative suppliers to quickly make up the lost supply is adding to tightness in the global gas market, and that competition between Europe and Asia, the world's two largest LNG-importing regions, for available cargoes is putting further upward pressure on prices. It gives the filling level of EU storage sites as 74.62% on 22 October, citing Gas Infrastructure Europe. The row does not give the benchmark contract, the price a year earlier, the storage level against the EU's target or against a year earlier, or any effect on industrial users or power prices.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a price, a statement on LNG volumes and a storage level, not a cost to industry. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, natural gas is both a fuel and a feedstock for the chemical industry, and a price at the highest level since December 2022 raises energy costs for producers that depend on it, with the effect set by their contracts and hedges. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the producers of resins, polymers and other raw materials use gas, so higher energy costs could pass into raw-material prices with a delay, while the row gives no figures for chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz, EU storage levels through the winter, and announcements of energy-cost surcharges by raw-material suppliers.

Anadolu Agency
